transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Dan Ronan.
The Justice Department has told the court that the U.S. Army will detonate close to five tons of bomb-making material
containing lead at a site in Iowa by Wednesday.
NPR's Andrea Shue reports.
At issue are 68 drums of what the U.S. Army says is significantly degraded
and unstable lead azide at a facility in Middletown, Iowa.
The Army has argued that because the material is at risk of exploding simultaneously,
a planned explosion would be safer.
It had planned to detonate the material on Friday, a week after the EPA granted the Army an emergency permit.
But two environmental groups sued to block that permit, citing irreparable health and environmental harm
and failure by the EPA to properly evaluate alternatives.
Last week, the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals temporarily suspended the permit.
Now, the Justice Department is arguing the Army does not need a permit
and says it intends to act on Wednesday.
Andrea Shue, NPR News.
Treasury Secretary Scott Besit says it's too soon to say whether former
NVIDIA CEO Jensen Wong should be returning to his leadership role.
He says it depends on the outcome of an investigation who sold advanced computer chips to China.
NPR's Shonda Lee Stuster reports.
Besit says NVIDIA has not answered questions about compliance after his previous demand to do so within 10 days.
On CBS News' Face the Nation, Besit said the Treasury Department has been in touch with the company's
temporary management and lawyers.
It behooves NVIDIA to move quickly on this because we want to know what the culture was.
Was there a promiscuous attitude toward this? And if it happened, where were the faults? And then they can move on.
Besit had previously said there was a, quote, "culture of non-compliance" at the company.
On Sunday, he said it's a possibility and that the board is moving quickly to determine if that exists.
Shonda Lee Stuster, NPR News.
A Russian flag ship that was hit and damaged Saturday by a suspected Ukrainian drone in the eastern Gulf of Finland is being towed away
after it apparently drifted into Finnish waters.
Terry Schultz reports.
Russia took control of this cargo ship, the Sparta II, and towed it out of Finnish waters a day after it was hit by a drone.
The crew was rescued by another Russian vessel traveling nearby at the time of the strike.
Now, the attack is presumed to have come from Ukraine, but Kyiv has not yet claimed responsibility.
Finnish President Alexander Stube referred to the incident as an "unfortunate reminder" that the, quote,
"consequences of Russia's war of aggression are also visible in our region."
It'll be a short week on Wall Street because of the Thanksgiving holiday Thursday.
Markets will be closed Thursday and open only until 1 p.m. on Friday.
All three indexes slumped last week amid concerns in the tech center. This is NPR.
The UN Climate Conference in Turkey has ended with no agreement among delegates over ways to combat the growing threat of climate change.
Representatives from Eastern European nations as well as Western European and climate-vulnerable nations, including Panama,
rejected a proposed agreement because they said it omitted transitioning away from fossil fuels.
Others blamed the oil industry, along with Russia and Saudi Arabia. The U.S. did not send a delegate.
New treatments like immunotherapy and stepped-up cancer screening continued to improve the survival rates from lung cancer.
NPR's Yuki Noguchi reports.
The American Lung Association's annual report finds 31 percent of lung cancer patients are still living five years after diagnosis.
That compares with 18 percent nine years ago.
The report speaks to rapid development in new treatments that target genetic mutations that drive cancer or immunotherapies that combat it.
New technologies like biomarker testing have also enabled treatment to become more personalized.
The survey found low-dose CT scanning rates increasing, but still below a quarter of those eligible.
Low smoking rates have also reduced incidence of lung cancer, but about 230,000 Americans will be diagnosed this year.
Yuki Noguchi, NPR News.
